research.headline: What's actually in a paycheck
points: Gross pay is the number you're quoted. Net pay — what hits your account — is smaller.
Taxes, and sometimes benefits, get taken out before you ever see the money.
A steady schedule (like retail) makes your net pay way easier to predict than gig work does.
research.tip: Whichever job you pick, always plan your budget around net pay, not the number in the posting.

research.headline: How a credit card actually works
points: A credit card is a loan you take out every time you swipe — not free money.
Pay the full statement balance by the due date and you owe $0 in interest, ever.
Pay only the minimum and the leftover balance racks up interest, often 20%+ a year.
research.tip: The habit that builds credit fastest: use it for something small, then pay it off in full.

research.headline: What's hiding in a lease
points: A security deposit is refundable — but only if you meet the conditions written in the lease.
Fees for things like 'amenities' or 'admin' are often negotiable if you ask before signing.
Anything you agree to in writing is what a landlord can legally hold you to — read every page.
research.tip: Skimming a lease can cost you more than the ten minutes it takes to actually read it.

research.headline: Why starting early beats saving more later
points: Compound interest means you earn returns on your returns, not just your original deposit.
An employer match is free money added on top of what you contribute — it's part of your pay.
Money invested in your 20s has decades to grow; the same amount at 40 has far less time.
research.tip: The real cost of skipping an IRA isn't the cash you kept — it's the growth that cash won't get to have.

research.headline: Why the first offer isn't the final offer
points: Most first offers have room built in — employers expect some back-and-forth.
Coming with specific reasons (results, added responsibilities) makes a counter hard to dismiss.
Asking doesn't damage your standing — declining to negotiate is what leaves money on the table.
research.tip: One successful negotiation early in your career compounds across every raise that follows it.

research.headline: What an emergency fund is actually for
points: An emergency fund is cash set aside only for real, unavoidable costs — not a want.
Paying cash for a surprise bill costs exactly the bill. Paying by credit adds interest on top.
The fund's job is to turn a crisis into an inconvenience.
research.tip: If a surprise bill would wreck your month, that's the signal to build this fund before anything else.

research.headline: What 'opportunity cost' really means
points: Opportunity cost is what you give up by choosing one option over another.
Saving isn't automatically the 'right' choice — money you never spend can't buy you anything either.
The real question isn't spend-or-save, it's 'what does this dollar do the most good doing?'
research.tip: A common blind spot is treating every purchase like a threat instead of asking what it's actually worth.

research.headline: Why where you keep cash matters
points: A typical checking account earns close to 0% interest — your money just sits there.
A high-yield savings account (HYSA) can earn 10–40x more with zero extra risk.
Moving money to a HYSA takes minutes and costs nothing — it's pure upside.
research.tip: Idle cash in checking isn't 'safe' — it's just not growing.

research.headline: Why minimum payments are a trap
points: Minimum payments are calculated to keep you paying interest for as long as possible.
Interest is charged on whatever balance is left — the longer it sits, the more it costs.
Paying more than the minimum (or paying it off in full) shrinks that interest fast.
research.tip: The 'minimum payment' number is set by the card company's interest, not by what's good for you.

research.headline: How subscriptions quietly add up
points: Small recurring charges don't feel like spending — which is exactly why they add up unnoticed.
A quick monthly audit usually finds at least one subscription you forgot you had.
Cancelling something is free. Not checking costs you every single month.
research.tip: Recurring charges are the easiest expense to fix, because the savings repeat too.

research.headline: Why an unfair split stays unfair
points: An arrangement doesn't become fair just because no one objected to it.
Money conversations feel awkward once — staying quiet costs you every month after.
Asking for a fair split is a negotiation, not a conflict.
research.tip: The discomfort of one conversation is usually smaller than the cost of avoiding it.

research.headline: Why 'it's not worth it' is worth checking
points: Money owed to you doesn't disappear just because collecting it is inconvenient.
Companies count on people not following up on refunds — it's often part of the business model.
A five-minute call for real money back is a strong hourly rate for 'annoying' work.
research.tip: Letting a small refund go teaches the same avoidance habit that costs more on bigger amounts.

research.headline: How to tell hype from a real opportunity
points: If everyone's suddenly talking about an investment, you're probably late, not early.
Fundamentals — what a thing is actually worth — move slowly. Hype moves fast, and reverses fast.
FOMO is a feeling, not information. It doesn't tell you anything about future price.
research.tip: By the time an investment is in every group chat, the easy gains are usually already gone.

research.headline: Why 'guaranteed' resale rarely is
points: Resale value depends on someone else wanting it later — that's a guess, not a guarantee.
Limited drops create artificial urgency designed to make you skip the math.
If everyone had the same idea to resell, there's rarely enough buyers for all of them.
research.tip: Buying extra of anything 'to flip' is a bet — go in knowing it's a bet.

research.headline: Why small repairs beat big ones
points: A small warning sign (like a check-engine light) usually costs far less to fix now than later.
Ignoring a problem doesn't make it go away — it usually makes it more expensive.
Preventive maintenance is one of the few costs that reliably saves you money over time.
research.tip: A small check-up now is cheap insurance against a much bigger repair later.

research.headline: Why one-off events need their own budget line
points: Events like weddings rarely have just one cost — flights, gifts, and outfits all add up.
Budgeting for the whole event ahead of time avoids surprise charges creeping in.
It's okay to scale your involvement to what you can actually afford, not what feels expected.
research.tip: The stress usually comes from the surprise, not the spending — plan the total ahead of time.

research.headline: How to weigh a cheap fix against a real one
points: The cheapest fix isn't always the cheapest option — it can fail again and cost you twice.
A quality repair usually comes with some guarantee; a bargain fix usually doesn't.
Compare cost per year of use, not just the sticker price of the repair.
research.tip: A repair that needs repeating isn't actually cheaper — it's the same bill, paid twice.

research.headline: Why the awkward conversation is the cheap option
points: Covering for someone quietly trains them to expect it — the pattern repeats.
A direct, low-key ask ('hey, did you get a chance to send that?') usually works.
You can be kind and still expect people to follow through on money commitments.
research.tip: The conversation costs you a little discomfort once. Covering it costs you money every time.

research.headline: How to start without overspending
points: A minimum viable product is the smallest version of your idea you can actually sell or test.
Courses and branding can wait — the fastest way to learn what works is a real customer.
Keep business money separate from personal money from day one, even informally.
research.tip: Most early 'startup costs' are optional. The one thing you can't skip is talking to a real customer.

research.headline: Why 'boring' investing usually wins
points: A diversified fund spreads your risk across hundreds of companies instead of betting on one.
Individual stock picks can outperform — but they can also go to zero. A fund almost never does.
Time in the market matters more than perfectly timing which stock to pick.
research.tip: The goal isn't to find the next big winner — it's to not need to.

research.headline: Why risk management beats hot tips
points: Position sizing means never risking more on one trade than you can afford to lose.
A stop-loss is a plan for being wrong, set before emotions get involved.
Most active traders underperform a simple buy-and-hold approach over time.
research.tip: The traders who last aren't the ones who are always right — they're the ones who lose small.

research.headline: Why a 'sinking fund' works better than hoping
points: A sinking fund is money set aside on purpose for one specific goal, kept separate from everyday cash.
Automating the transfer means the saving happens before you have a chance to spend it.
A vague goal ('save more') is much easier to abandon than a specific one with a number and a date.
research.tip: Money you never see in your main account is money you're far less likely to spend.

research.headline: What actually moves your credit score
points: Credit utilization — how much of your limit you're using — is one of the biggest score factors.
Keeping utilization under 30%, and ideally lower, tends to help your score the most.
On-time payments matter even more than utilization — the two together do most of the work.
research.tip: Paying down your balance before the statement closes (not just before it's due) is what actually lowers reported utilization.

research.headline: A simple way to split any paycheck
points: The 50/30/20 rule: roughly 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings or debt payoff, as a starting point.
'Paying yourself first' means moving savings out before you budget the rest.
A simple plan you'll actually follow beats a perfect budget you'll abandon in a week.
research.tip: You don't need a perfect system — you need a simple one you'll still be using in three months.
